opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I should say upfront that I don't think pre-training is "solved" or uninteresting. It's still the foundation everything else sits on. But from a practical research perspective, I think post-training is where a lot of the interesting, accessible progress is happening right now.

Part of it is just economics. Pre-training a competitive base model takes enormous compute, huge curated datasets, and a big engineering team. Most researchers in academia, smaller labs, or companies outside the top handful simply can't run those experiments. And even if you can, the feedback loop is slow. You might wait weeks to find out whether an idea worked. Post-training is different. You can take a strong open-weight base model and run meaningful experiments on a single node, or sometimes even a single GPU, and see results in hours or days. That faster iteration cycle means more people can contribute and more ideas get tested.

The second reason is that we've seen how much capability post-training actually unlocks. Early on, people thought of instruction fine-tuning and RLHF as polishing: making the model friendlier and better at following a chat format. Over the last couple of years, especially with reasoning models trained with reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards, it became clear that post-training can substantially change what a model can do. A lot of the latent ability is already in the base model from pre-training, and post-training is about drawing it out, shaping it, and teaching the model to use more compute at inference time to think through problems. Math, coding, multi-step reasoning: the jumps we've seen there came largely from post-training recipes.

Third, there are still a lot of open questions on the post-training side, which makes it fertile ground. How do you design good reward signals for tasks that aren't easily verifiable? How much supervised fine-tuning data do you need before RL, or can you skip it? How do you avoid reward hacking, or keep reasoning traces from getting unnecessarily long? How do distillation from a larger model and RL compare for smaller models? Those are questions you can actually study empirically without a billion-dollar budget.

And on pre-training, some of the low-hanging fruit has been picked. Scaling laws are fairly well understood, architectures have converged a lot (most models are variations on the same decoder-only transformer with tweaks like grouped-query attention, mixture-of-experts, and different normalization choices), and high-quality data is becoming a bottleneck. There's still important work there, on data quality, efficiency, and architecture, but the marginal research return for most people is higher on the post-training side.

So I'd put it this way: pre-training gives you the raw material, and post-training is increasingly where you decide what the model becomes. And it's the part of the pipeline where a much broader research community can make a real contribution.

r001.rationale: The response says post-training recipes produced major capability gains and that its marginal research return is higher than pre-training’s, supporting greater scope for gains from post-training methods.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the short version is that pre-training has become a game that very few people can actually play, and post-training is where you can still do interesting, meaningful work without a data center.

If you look at pre-training today, the frontier labs are spending tens or hundreds of millions of dollars on a single run. Even at the academic scale, if you want to train something that's competitive, you're talking about hundreds of GPUs for weeks. And the ideas there, honestly, have converged quite a bit. The architecture is mostly a decoder-only transformer with some variations, maybe mixture-of-experts, maybe some tweaks to attention. The recipe is fairly well understood, and the remaining gains are largely about scale and data quality. That's important work, but it's not where a researcher with a small lab or an individual is going to make a difference.

Post-training is different. You can take a strong open-weight base model, something like a Llama or a Qwen or an OLMo, and with a few GPUs, or sometimes even one, you can meaningfully change how that model behaves. And we've seen over the last couple of years that this is where a lot of the capability gains are actually coming from. The jump to reasoning models, for example, is largely a post-training story. The base models didn't change that dramatically. What changed is that people figured out how to use reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, things like math problems and code with unit tests, to get the model to produce longer, more deliberate reasoning traces. And the DeepSeek R1 paper in particular showed that you could do this with a relatively simple recipe. That opened up a whole space of questions that are still unanswered.

So, how much supervised fine-tuning do you actually need before RL? Does the reasoning behavior transfer across domains? What are the right reward signals when you don't have a verifier? How do you avoid the model becoming verbose and overthinking simple questions? Those are all things you can study at a scale that's accessible, and the results actually inform what the big labs do too.

The other thing I'd say is that post-training is where the model meets the user. Pre-training gives you a model that has absorbed a lot of knowledge, but it's not useful on its own. Everything that makes it helpful, safe, able to follow instructions, able to use tools, that's all post-training. So from a practical standpoint, if you care about making models that people actually use, that's where the leverage is.

I don't want to say pre-training is solved, because it clearly isn't. Data efficiency is a big open question, and there's interesting work on synthetic data and curriculum. But if someone asked me where to spend their time as a researcher right now, especially with limited compute, I'd point them toward post-training without much hesitation.

r001.rationale: The response says pre-training ideas have converged and remaining gains largely depend on scale and data quality, while post-training has produced major capability gains and still has unanswered questions about methods such as RL and reward signals. This communicates greater opportunity for gains through post-training algorithmic changes.

astra-6.text:
I think a big part of it is the room for experimentation. Pre-training is still important, but if you want to study it at the frontier, you need enormous amounts of compute and data. That makes it difficult for a smaller research group to try an idea, run good comparisons, and iterate.

With post-training, you can start from a strong open-weight model and ask: How do we make better use of what this model has already learned? How do we make it follow instructions more reliably, or improve its reasoning through reinforcement learning? You still need compute, but the experiments are much more accessible than training a model from scratch.

And there are a lot of open questions. What should you reward? How much does the quality of the training examples matter? Are you teaching the model a new capability, or helping it express something it could already do? Those are interesting scientific questions with very practical consequences.

So I wouldn’t say pre-training is solved. It’s more that, right now, post-training gives you a really compelling combination of research opportunity, accessibility, and potential impact.

r001.rationale: The response describes post-training as more accessible and open to experimentation, including improving reasoning with reinforcement learning, but does not say it offers greater performance gains from algorithmic changes than pre-training.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a big part of it is accessibility. If you want to study pre-training at the frontier, you need enormous amounts of data and compute. That makes it difficult for a university lab or a small research team to run experiments and really test ideas.

With post-training, you can start with an existing pretrained model and investigate how to make it more useful—through instruction tuning, preference optimization, or reinforcement learning. You still need compute, but the barrier to doing meaningful experiments is much lower.

And there are a lot of open questions. How do you choose the training data? How do you design a reward that encourages the behavior you actually want? How do you improve reasoning without degrading other capabilities? I wouldn’t say pre-training is solved, but post-training gives more researchers an opportunity to make substantial contributions with the resources they have.

r001.rationale: The response says post-training has open questions and allows more researchers to contribute, but it does not identify greater room for performance gains from algorithmic changes in post-training than in pre-training.
